profile.reading:
Per Flexential's own individual facility page, this building (Flexential Charlotte - North) is located at 10105 David Taylor Drive, Charlotte, NC 28262. The operator publishes a footprint of 62589 square feet and 3.3 MW of critical load UPS capacity for this specific building, with published certifications and compliance attestations including SOC 1 Type 2, SOC 2 Type 2, PCI DSS, HIPAA, ISO 27001, SSAE 18. North Carolina's data center demand has grown sharply: Duke Energy's projected additional capacity need rose from about 3.9 gigawatts in early 2024 to nearly 6 gigawatts by May 2025, roughly equivalent to four nuclear plants, according to Canary Media's reporting. Major projects driving that growth include Amazon Web Services' $10 billion, 800-acre campus in Richmond County, billed as the largest single capital project in North Carolina history; an Apple site in Catawba County included in the company's broader $500 billion US expansion; four new Microsoft data centers planned near Charlotte; and an expansion of Google's Caldwell County facility. Duke has won regulatory approval for a large new fleet of gas plants despite state decarbonization requirements, prompting a policy debate among clean-energy advocates who favor load flexibility, utility-scale solar and battery storage, virtual power plants, and clean-transition tariffs as alternatives; a North Carolina Utilities Commission proceeding was scheduled for October 2025 to examine these competing approaches, with timeline pressure driven partly by neighboring Virginia's data center construction pace of 18 months or less.

Duke Energy has separately sought a 15% North Carolina rate increase over two years, on top of bills that had already risen about 22% since 2020, and data centers, currently less than 1% of peak energy use but projected to eventually account for roughly 80% of future demand growth and about 30% of upcoming development projects statewide, have become central to the resulting rate debate, per reporting citing Environmental Defense Fund policy director Will Scott. Scott has argued new power plants built to serve data centers should be paid for through special fees on those large customers rather than socialized across all ratepayers, while Duke spokesperson Bill Norton has disputed that data centers are driving the increases, attributing them instead to infrastructure maintenance and arguing that industrial growth broadly helps spread fixed costs over a larger customer base.

[batch narration moved out of reading 2026-09-02] This Flexential cluster spans Georgia (Alpharetta, Douglasville, Norcross), Florida (Fort Lauderdale, Jacksonville, Tampa), North Carolina (Charlotte, Morrisville), and Tennessee (Brentwood, Franklin), the historic Southeastern United States footprint of Peak 10. According to Flexential own company history page, Peak 10 was founded in 2000 and built a strong regional presence across the Southeastern US. In 2017 Peak 10 purchased ViaWest, merging the two regionally dominant data center providers, and the combined company rebranded as Flexential in 2018. Flexential also acquired AppliedTrust and INetU in 2015 to expand its professional services and cloud offerings. Flexential operates 40 plus data centers across 18 national markets under CEO Ryan Mallory. reading.body:
Flexential Charlotte North has 3.3 MW of published IT capacity, ranking third among North Carolina facilities with disclosed power figures and representing 6.6 percent of the state's 50.3 MW of published data center capacity. At typical AI training density of 6 MW per 1,000 accelerators, this facility could support approximately 550 accelerators, though the operator publishes no specification of actual rack density or accelerator count.

The facility holds certifications for compliance with financial services standards, healthcare privacy regulations, and information security frameworks: SOC 1 Type 2, SOC 2 Type 2, PCI DSS, HIPAA, ISO 27001, and SSAE 18. These certifications qualify the campus to host regulated workloads but do not indicate which tenants are present or whether any are AI training operations.

North Carolina has 19 mapped data center facilities but only five publish power capacity figures, leaving substantial unquantified infrastructure. This Charlotte campus sits within a nine-state Flexential footprint built on the historic Peak 10 regional network. Whether this regional clustering advantages AI workload placement or grid access in the Southeast remains unpublished and therefore unknown from available sources.
